messages.body_plain:
Thank you for your help. While this is certainly the correct approach I ran into some trouble because my model is more complex than let on. Below is my full model statement:

formula.p <- y14 ~ 1 + f(ID, model = "bym", graph = Cnty3109.adj, constr = TRUE, scale.model = TRUE) +
                            f(countyTrend, YearNum, model = "iid", constr = TRUE) +
                            factor(STATE) +
                            factor(YearNum) +
                            factor(RUCC) +
                            s.pct.0_19 +
                            s.pct.20_44 +
                            s.pct.45_64 +
                            s.pct.male +
                            s.pct.nhwhite +
                            s.pct.nhblack +
                            s.pct.hispanic +
                            s.pct.hs_less +
                            s.pct.collegeplus +
                           # mydata14$UNEMPRATE_cat1 +
                          #  mydata14$UNEMPRATE_cat2 +
                          #  mydata14$UNEMPRATE_cat3 +
                            s.SPOPDENS +
                            proportion_of_year_mml_effect +
                            must_access +
                            s.gini +
                            s.PO.supply +
                            PO_supply_X_ineq
                          #  (mydata14$s.PO.supply*mydata14$UNEMPRATE_cat1) +
                          #  (mydata14$s.PO.supply*mydata14$UNEMPRATE_cat2) +
                          #  (mydata14$s.PO.supply*mydata14$UNEMPRATE_cat3)

Sys.time()  # Show system time just to keep track of how long INLA is taking

mod.p <- inla(formula.p, family = c("poisson"),

                    data=mydata14, E=e14,
                    control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE, config = TRUE),
                    control.inla=list(tolerance=1e-20, h=1e-6),
                    control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE)

                    )

As such, am I correct in assuming that I will need to remove the terms based on all the covariates, including the two factor variables, state which has 49 levels and year which has 10 levels.

If so, I can remove the terms for the continuous variables with ease, but I'm unsure how to remove the terms based on the factor variables. Is there an trick to removing factor variables? Or, will I need to remove them one at a time for each level?

Also, is it possible to get the same value through a linear combination? I was thinking a linear combination would be specified as:

Lincomb_lc1=inla.make.lincomb("PO_supply_X_ineq"=1, "s.gini"=1, "s.PO.supply"=1, "s.gini"=-1, "s.PO.supply"=-1)
names(Lincomb_lc1) = "Lincomb_lc1"

But, I need to exponentiate each term before subtracting the independent variables (ie., s.gini, s.PO.supply) from the interaction term (i.e., PO_supply_X_ineq).

Any guidance is greatly appreciated.

Thank you for your help.

automatic expansion, like

> model.matrix( ~ x, data = data.frame(x = as.factor(c("a", "b", 1)))
+ )
  (Intercept) xa xb
1           1  1  0
2           1  0  1
3           1  0  0
attr(,"assign")
[1] 0 1 1
attr(,"contrasts")
attr(,"contrasts")$x
[1] "contr.treatment"

also find in

	result$misc$configs$contents

there is another line of trick which is sometimes useful, which comes
with a little cost, but simplifies life, is to construct the linear
predictor to contain what you want with no data. but often my time is
more important than the computer's so...

here is an example. maybe you can do it along these lines?

x = rnorm(n)
fac = as.factor(1:10)

r = inla(y ~ 1 + x + fac, data = data.frame(y, x, fac))
summary(r)

but I can also use
## another trick. I just add a fake model with no data, where the
linear predictor are these
## using NA, like

xx = c(rep(NA, n),  x)
ffac = c(fac, fac)
yy = c(rep(NA, n), y)
rr = inla(yy ~ 1 + xx + ffac, data = data.frame(yy, xx, ffac),
          control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE))
summary(rr)

## and then

rr$summary.linear.predictor$mean[1:n]

the reponse

df = data.frame(....whatever...)

messages.body_plain:
H,

Are there any general guidelines for how and when tweaking the tolerance / convergence values may make sense, particularly if one is concerned about initial values resulting in different convergence points?

For example, in Virgilio’s book, he occasionally suggests modifying the control.inla statement to this:

control.inla = list(tolerance = 1e-20, h = 1e-4)

That appears to loosen the default tolerance threshold but tighten the h threshold and it is not automatically clear to me why this combination or moving either value would necessarily be desirable.

Getting consistent results with different initial values is my primary concern, and I recognize that may in fact be also / better addressed with priors, but perhaps there is a practical range of tolerance values usually worth trying that won’t necessarily also create instability issues?

Thank you,

Jonathan

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

in general, you can set the tolerance lower, as if its to low then
other criteria (like ``fail to improve'' in the optimizer will kick in
instead). sometimes this is useful with very flat posteriors. but often
its better just to rerun, like

	r = inla(....)
	r = inla.rerun(r)

if the posterior is flat. but better again, is to fix the model...

'h' is different. its the step-size for the hyperparameter in the
gradient calculations, and sqrt(h) is the step-size for the hessian
calculations. if that is to low, then these becomes inaccurate. its
better with to high than to low. default is

> inla.set.control.inla.default()$h
[1] 0.01

I would not go much lower than 0.001. Also, if the model is large, then
its even more important that h is not to low, as, cholesky
factorisations and like log determinants computed from those, are not
accurate in all digits.

consistent results: this is only possible if running in serial mode,
like

	inla(..., num.threads=1)

when running in parallel, by the way its implemented, you'll never get
fully identical results (in all digits). this is a feature not a bug.

like

> print(inla(y~f(i),data=data.frame(y,i=1:n),family="poisson")$mlik)
                                              [,1]
log marginal-likelihood (integration) -1927.456417 <<<<<======
log marginal-likelihood (Gaussian)    -1927.557029
> print(inla(y~f(i),data=data.frame(y,i=1:n),family="poisson")$mlik)
                                              [,1]
log marginal-likelihood (integration) -1927.456418 <<<<<======
log marginal-likelihood (Gaussian)    -1927.557029

you see the ...7 and ...8.

while

>
print(inla(y~f(i),data=data.frame(y,i=1:n),family="poisson",num.threads
=1)$mlik)
                                              [,1]
log marginal-likelihood (integration) -1927.456391
log marginal-likelihood (Gaussian)    -1927.556800
>
print(inla(y~f(i),data=data.frame(y,i=1:n),family="poisson",num.threads
=1)$mlik)
                                              [,1]
log marginal-likelihood (integration) -1927.456391
log marginal-likelihood (Gaussian)    -1927.556800

H

messages.subject_clean: parametric link
messages.body_plain:
I am wondering if it is possible to “parametrize” a link function – i.e. to add some parameters to it and estimate them in INLA. This is motivated by the 4-parameter logistic model (also known as the Hill model) that has been used in toxicology and other contexts. My motivation comes from educational testing where probability of correct answer (pi) to yes/no question is modelled via logistic regression with some measure of ability as the explanatory variable (x) and the additional two parameters correspond to probability of correct guessing (c) and probability of incorrect answer due to inattention (d). There we have a link log((pi-c)/(d-pi)).
I am thinking about expanding usual logistic link (but obviously, the same thing can be done to others) by introducing c and d parameters and estimating them by INLA (we already have several frequentist methods here).

My question is whether (and how) I can modify the link function. Then I was planning either to evaluate the model on a grid of c,d values and use Bayesian model averaging or INLA-within-MCMC ideas from Virgilio Gomez-Rubio’s book (chapter 11). Or, is there a more direct way to let INLA estimate c,d?

All the Best
 Marek

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marek,

I'll let Haavard answer about R-INLA itself, but this type of problem
is something we're experimenting with in the inlabru package.
inlabru takes general R expressions as non-linear predictors, and
iterates linearised version with R-INLA. For example (for illustration
only),
if one wanted to have a probit link with coupled expectation and
variance parameters, one could do ask for a regular logit link, but
define the nonlinear expression through

  formula = y ~ logit(pnorm(linear_predictor, mean = par1, sd = exp(par2)))

where linear_predictor would be what you'd normally have after the ~
in your INLA formula. Then the model components would be specified (in
the case of only fixed covariates) as

  comp = ~ Intercept + covar1 + covar2 + par1 + par2

where par1 and par2 wouldn't exist in your input data frame, and the
current version interprets that as "new" intercept parameters. (a bit
more code needed if one needs to specify other priors than regular
covariate effects have, and a future version will have slightly
different syntax for clarity, likely just "par1(1) + par2(1)")

Then  linear_predictor above should be   Intercept + covar1 + covar2.

inlabru then treats the unknown parameters par1 and par2 as other
latent Gaussian parameters. The result isn't as accurate as full INLA
approximation, but it does allow reasonable approximation of more
generalised nonlinear models.

The current inlabru release can be a bit unstable in the iterations if
the predictor is too nonlinear, but we have workshop examples on
inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org> that use this feature for other types of nonlinearities.

I'm currently busy with coronavirus software coding, but hope to
finish the next major inlabru release (that should resolve the
iteration instabilities and clean up the interface) in the coming few
months.

Finn L, Edinburgh

messages.body_plain:
Marek, thanks for your email. INLA can have link-models, so link-
functions that contains parameters that are estimated along with
others. In this case, the parameters of the link function will be part
of the hyperparameters, so, of'course, we would need to keep that
number down.

The model you're seeking is the sensitivity/specificity `link' where
the proportion you see in the data would be

	prob = sens * q + (1-spec)*(1-q)

for fixed sens and spec, and

	logit(q) = linear predictor

Although its implemented (but not documented), there are 'issues' with
this, as the Hessian of log(prob) as a function of the linear
predictor, is pretty bad. If you plot it, you would see. very much
worse than I thought, and to the point that I question if we're able at
all to give reliable estimates of this model. I really really wished
this was not the case, but I have no work-around. [unless 'spec=1',
of'course].

if you're in the case where prob is either very low or high, then its
much better, as the case where is about similar likely that a positive
outcome could either be a true positive, or a false negative, would
(almost) not happen. This is the source for the problem.

Then the other issue, is that, even with knowledge of the sens and
spec, they are, by design, not informative from the data! You may put a
prior on them and try to estimate them and account for their
uncertainty, but there will be feedback, hence the posteriors for
sens/spec will not be equal to the prior. It has to be, as the data are
not informative about them. How much depends also on the model error.
So you have put approach this problem differently, see f.ex Cuts in
Bayesian graphical models, Martyn Plummer, Statistics and Computing,
2015. and we have tools to do that as well, see ?inla.merge . In this
way you can propagate a known uncertinaty about sens/spec throughout
the analysis, without feedback, but you have to know the distributions
of sens/spec upfront.

Sorry for this rather 'negative' answer

H

messages.body_plain:
yes, one can think of ways to estimate sens/spec, of'course.

here is an example

se = 0.9; sp = 0.9
q = function(eta) 1/(1+exp(-eta))
p = function(eta) se * q(eta) + (1-sp)*(1-q(eta))
eta = seq(-5,5,by=0.01)
par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
fun = splinefun(eta, log(p(eta)))
plot(eta, fun(eta))
plot(eta, fun(eta, deriv=2))
abline(a=0, b=0)

messages.subject: marginal random effects vs summary random effects for disease mapping
messages.subject_clean: marginal random effects vs summary random effects for disease mapping
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I fit a space-time interaction model for an infectious disease. I have 397 areas (census tracts) and 19 years of data. The data is quite sparse with plenty of zeros in the I*T matrix.

This is the model with Type 1 interaction between space and time:

formula.intI<- y ~ + f(ID.area,model="bym",graph="/Users/mrane/Desktop/KC2010.graph")+ f(ID.year,model="iid")+
  f(ID.year1,model="rw2") + f(ID.area.year,model="iid")

mod.intI <- inla(formula.intI,family="poisson",data=casebyCT.data,E=E,
                 control.predictor=list(link=1,compute=TRUE),
                 control.inla=list(int.strategy='eb'),
                 control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

The main purpose of this exercise is disease mapping. I would like map disease risk smoothed in space and time over 19 years. My question is: should I plot the mod.intI$marginals.random$ID.area (marginal random effects) or mod.intI$summary.random$ID.area (summary of random effects)? I have seen both used to display heterogeneity in spatial risk. The maps look very different depending on which of those I plot. ICAR spatial random effects are almost non-existent, while there is good variation in marginal random effects.

Thanks!

messages.subject: INLA error when I use a smaller grid?
messages.subject_clean: INLA error when I use a smaller grid?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I am examining the sensitivity of my results to the scale (grain) of analysis, and can get INLA to work for larger scales (50 km to 100 km grid cell widths), but not for my smallest scale (24 km). Though I have the latest / testing version of INLA installed, I can't seem to get an informative error message. I have attached input data and code, and wondered if you could tell me what is going wrong? Does it have to do with the small grid size?

Thank you for your help!

##################################################

library(INLA)

sp_counts= read.table('sample_counts.txt',sep='\t',as.is <http://as.is>=T,check.names=F,header=T)
g1 <- inla.read.graph('./nb24.graph') #graph network of grid neighbors

# Transform effort & standardize years
sp_counts$ln.Person.hours = log(sp_counts$Person.hours)
sp_counts$std_Year = sp_counts$Year - max(sp_counts$Year)

# Index and sort
sp_counts$eps_i <- sp_counts$alpha_i <- sp_counts$grid_id
sp_counts$tau_i <- sp_counts$eps_i
sp_counts$kappa_k <- as.integer(factor(sp_counts$Site))
sp_counts <- arrange(sp_counts, grid_id, std_Year)

# Make negative binomial model with raw counts
form1 <- N.butterflies ~ -1 + # remove grand mean
  # cell ICAR random intercepts
  f(alpha_i, model="besag", graph=g1, constr=FALSE, scale.model=TRUE, hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)))) +
  # cell ICAR random effort slopes
  f(eps_i, ln.Person.hours, model="besag", graph=g1, constr=FALSE, scale.model=TRUE, hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)))) +
  # cell ICAR random year slopes
  f(tau_i, std_Year, model="besag", graph=g1, constr=FALSE, scale.model=TRUE, hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)))) +
  # random circle intercepts
  f(kappa_k, model="iid", constr=TRUE, hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01))))

# Run model
out1 <- inla(form1, family="nbinomial", data=sp_counts, control.compute=list(cpo=T, config=T), control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive", int.strategy="auto"), num.threads=3, debug=TRUE, silent=FALSE)

##################################################

messages.subject: Specifying stack for mec (classical measurement error) model
messages.subject_clean: Specifying stack for mec (classical measurement error) model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm performing spatial regression in R-INLA on a predictor measured with error, and with SPDE random effects for space. I would like to use the mec model for the predictor in question, however I'm running into an issue that I think has to do with how I've specified the stack.

My code is:
A<-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=HAT@coords)
iset <- inla.spde.make.index('i', n.spde=spde_RE$n.spde)
stk.dat<-inla.stack(
  data=list(resp=HAT@data$cases),
  A=list(A,1),
  effects=list(c(iset, list(intercept=1)), list(HAT@data)),
  tag='est')
formula<- resp ~ -1 + intercept + f(dens, model="mec", scale=d.WP, values=dens_x,
hyper=list(beta=list(prior="gaussian", param= beta.prior fixed=FALSE),prec.u=list(prior="loggamma", param=lgamma.prior, initial=log(init.prec.u), fixed=FALSE),mean.x=list(prior="gaussian", initial=init.mean, fixed=TRUE),prec.x=list(prior="loggamma", param=lgamma.prior, initial=log(init.prec.x), fixed=FALSE))) + elevation + f(i, model=spde_RE) + f(cluster, model='iid', param=hyperpc1)

res<-inla (formula, data=inla.stack.data(stk.dat), family="zeroinflatedpoisson1", offset=log(HAT@data$WorldPop), control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.dat)),
              num.threads = inla.getOption("num.threads"),
              control.compute=list(config = TRUE)),TRUE)

This is the error I get:

Error in inla(formula, data = inla.stack.data(stk.dat), family = "zeroinflatedpoisson1",  :
  The 'values' given in f(dens,..., values=...) are not unique:
    length(values)=2888 but length(unique(values))=2803

dens_x is just dens with small gaussian (N(0, 10e-10)) noise added to all values are unique. There are 612 mesh nodes and 2,802 rows in HAT@data, but 2888 rows in stk.dat$effects$data, with the first 86 of these being NA for all but i, i.group, and i.repl.

Any idea what I've done wrong/how to fix this?

Thanks,
Julianne

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I just wonder if there is confusion between 'dens' and 'dens_x',
in the model component

	f(dens,"mec", values=dens_x)

dens must be a subset of dens_x, and all values of dens must be in
dens_x, please see inla.doc("mec")

'dens' gives the values of the observed covariates, and two identical
values defines the *same* missing covariate. so this is why a tiny
noise can be added if this is not the case.

maybe you do not need to add the argument 'values=dens_x'

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
I agree with Haavard,
With the addition that if your dens_x variable exists in the data frame given to inla.stack, the result will not be what the values parameter needs, so make sure it’s not in there.

Finn

> On 15 Apr 2020, at 19:31, Helpdesk <he...@r-inla.org> wrote:
>
> ﻿Hi,

>
> I just wonder if there is confusion between 'dens' and 'dens_x',
> in the model component
>
>    f(dens,"mec", values=dens_x)
>
>
> dens must be a subset of dens_x, and all values of dens must be in
> dens_x, please see inla.doc("mec")
>
> 'dens' gives the values of the observed covariates, and two identical
> values defines the *same* missing covariate. so this is why a tiny
> noise can be added if this is not the case.
>
> maybe you do not need to add the argument 'values=dens_x'
>
> Best
> H
>
>
>
>

For all the random effects models it represents for which values of the given covariate the internal model should be built. It’s rarely needed, since the default is to use all of the unique values.

I haven’t worked with the mec model myself, but have used values with e.g. ar1 models, where values needed to be specified to fill in a missing timepoint in a timeseries model that happened to not have any data.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Specifying stack for mec (classical measurement error) model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Specifying stack for mec (classical measurement error) model
messages.body_plain:
I think 'mec' is one of the models where it make less sense to define
'values'.  in general

	f(v, ..., values=val)

defines for which 'values' the model is defined for (which is context
spesific), and v is which of those that are used.

often, the usage is implicite, like

	f(time, model="ar1")

for which the ar1 process is defined for time=1:100

however, if time = c(1,2,4,5), then this does NOT mean that time 4 is
two lags behind time 2, as the process is defined for these values and
the AR1 does not have a concept of 'distance' beyond unity. [there is
the 'ou' model for this case. here, 'values' comes in handy, by
defining explictely for which values the model is defined, like

f(time, model="ar1", values = 1:100)

for which time = c(1,2,4,5) has the 'correct' meaning.

another example is this

y = c(1,0,2)
x = c(1,2,4)
plot(x,y, pch=19, xlim=c(0,5), ylim = c(0,5))
xx = seq(0,5,by=0.1)

r = inla(y ~ -1 + f(x, model="rw2", constr=F,values = xx), data =
list(y=y,x=x,xx=xx), control.family = list(hyper=list(prec
list(initial=20,fixed=TRUE))))

lines(xx, r$summary.random$x$mean)
points(xx, r$summary.random$x$mean)

in the 'mec' case, 'values' defines the set of possible  observed
covariates, for which some are used.

H

messages.subject: Piecewise Cox proportional hazards regression using INLA
messages.subject_clean: Piecewise Cox proportional hazards regression using INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hello colleagues,

I'm developing a Cox proportional hazards model for time to event data where the proportional hazards assumption is violated. To deal with this I'd like to develop a piecewise Cox model. I'm looking for some advice re how to do this correctly using INLA.

Attached to this message is a copy of the Caplehorn and Bell (1991) addict data which can be used as a minimum working example. The addict data set records the time individuals receiving treatment at two clinics returned to drug use. The explanatory variables for this study are: (1) clinic [Clinic 1 = 1; Clinic 2 = 2]; (2) prison [prison record absent = 0; prison record present = 1]; and (3) dose [maximum daily methadone dose, in milligrams].

Here's the code I've used for the analysis using the survival package in R:

library(survival)
dat <- read.table("addict.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",")

# Create a piecewise data set, partitioning into before 365 days and after 365 days:
dat.cp <- survSplit(data = dat, cut = 365, end = "stop", event = "status", start = "start", id = "iid")

# Recode clinic, making clinic 2 the reference:
dat.cp$rclinic <- ifelse(dat.cp$clinic == 2, 0, 1)

t1 <- rep(0, nrow(dat.cp))
t1[dat.cp$stop <= 365] <- 1
dat.cp$t1 <- t1

t2 <- rep(0, nrow(dat.cp))
t2[dat.cp$stop > 365] <- 1
dat.cp$t2 <- t2

# Create a Surv object:
addict.sur02 <- Surv(dat.cp$start, dat.cp$stop, event = dat.cp$status, type = "counting")

# Cox model:
addict.cph02 <- coxph(addict.sur02 ~ prison + dose + I(rclinic * t1) + I(rclinic * t2), method = "breslow", data = dat.cp)
round(summary(addict.cph02)$coefficients, digits = 4)

# Results:
#                   coef exp(coef)  se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)
# prison          0.3651    1.4406   0.1684  2.1681   0.0302
# dose           -0.0353    0.9653   0.0064 -5.5054   0.0000
# I(clinic * t1)  0.4802    1.6164   0.2548  1.8842   0.0595
# I(clinic * t2)  1.8122    6.1236   0.3864  4.6904   0.0000

Interpretation: The daily hazard of relapse for patients from clinic 1 before 365 days was exp(0.4802) = 1.6 times that of patients from clinic 2 before 365 days. The daily hazard of relapse for patients from clinic 1 after 365 days was exp(1.8122) = 6.1 times that of patients from clinic 2 before 365 days.

My question is, how can I reproduce this analysis using INLA to produce two hazard ratio estimates for the effect of clinic for each time period? Here's where I've got so far:

dat <- read.table("addict.csv", header = TRUE, sep = ",")
dat$rclinic <- ifelse(dat$clinic == 2, 0, 1)

t1 <- rep(0, nrow(dat))
t1[dat$stop <= 365] <- 1
dat$t1 <- t1

t2 <- rep(0, nrow(dat))
t2[dat$stop > 365] <- 1
dat$t2 <- t2

addict.isur02 <- inla.surv(time = dat$stop, event = dat$status)

# I'm assuming the cutpoints argument in control.hazard can be used to create a piecewise data set. Is this correct?

addict.icph02 <- inla(addict.isur02 ~ 1 + prison + dose + I(rclinic * t1) + I(rclinic * t2), family = "coxph",
   control.hazard = list(model = "rw1", cutpoints = c(0,365,1076)), data = dat)
round(addict.icph02$summary.fixed, digits = 4)

# Results:
                   mean      sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant    mode   kld
(Intercept)     -4.2818 53.0495  -115.4529  -4.2021   106.4649 -4.1076 5e-04
prison           0.2930  0.1664    -0.0349   0.2933     0.6184  0.2941 0e+00
dose            -0.0334  0.0062    -0.0454  -0.0334    -0.0213 -0.0334 0e+00
I(rclinic * t1)  1.8551  0.2871     1.3121   1.8477     2.4404  1.8331 0e+00
I(rclinic * t2)  0.5879  0.2372     0.1320   0.5847     1.0627  0.5783 0e+00

The coefficients for I(rclinic * t1) and I(rclinic * t2) look like they're the reverse of the coefficients from the survival package analysis. What am I doing wrong?

Many thanks in advance for any help you can provide.

Regards,

Mark Stevenson

Thanks so much for the speedy reply Håvard!

Analysis of the addict data using the survival package:

addict.cph02 <- coxph(addict.sur02 ~ prison + dose + I(rclinic * t1) + I(rclinic * t2), method = "breslow", data = dat.cp)
round(summary(addict.cph02)$coefficients, digits = 4)

# Results:
#                   coef exp(coef)  se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)
# prison          0.3651    1.4406   0.1684  2.1681   0.0302
# dose           -0.0353    0.9653   0.0064 -5.5054   0.0000
# I(clinic * t1)  0.4802    1.6164   0.2548  1.8842   0.0595
# I(clinic * t2)  1.8122    6.1236   0.3864  4.6904   0.0000

The same, using your suggestions in INLA:

dat$strata <- t2 + 1

addict.isur02 <- inla.surv(time = dat$stop, event = dat$status)

addict.icph02 <- inla(addict.isur02 ~ 1 + prison + dose + I(rclinic * t1) + I(rclinic * t2), family = "coxph",

   control.hazard = list(model = "rw2", cutpoints = c(0,365,1076), strata.name <http://strata.name> = "strata"), data = dat)
round(addict.icph02$summary.fixed, digits = 4)

#                    mean     sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant    mode    kld
# (Intercept)     -7.8006 2.7766   -14.3195  -7.5068    -3.2095 -7.2331 0.0245
# prison           0.0528 0.1702    -0.2823   0.0531     0.3858  0.0538 0.0000
# dose            -0.0170 0.0066    -0.0300  -0.0170    -0.0041 -0.0170 0.0000
# I(rclinic * t1)  0.0361 0.2558    -0.4469   0.0292     0.5584  0.0155 0.0000
# I(rclinic * t2)  1.6397 0.3740     0.9548   1.6219     2.4241  1.5860 0.0000

So the survival package gives hazard ratios of exp(0.4802) = 1.62 for period 1 and exp(1.8122) = 6.12. INLA gives hazard ratios of exp(0.0361) = 1.04 for period 1 and exp(1.6397) = 5.15 for period 2. Close enough?

As you suggest, I'll check with some simulated data.

Thanks again.

Mark S

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Prior for spatial length-scale?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Prior for spatial length-scale?
messages.body_plain:
For pc-prior for SPDE matern models, see
?inla.spde.pcmatern
By design, that one doesn’t have any default parameters for the prior.
The documentation explains the parameters.

The inla.spde.matern models use a log-gaussian prior for tau and kappa, with prior mean zero. I recommend agains using the default parameters (that feature is only still there for backwards compatibility). Instead, see the approach in the journal of statistical software, Lindgren&Rue “Bayesian Spatial Modelling with R-INLA”.
You can find this on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>, under
“Examples and tutorials”-“Tutorials”-“Read this first!”

Finn

aaah, this is very different from what I understood earlier.  if you
have fixed effects

	y ~ .... + x1 + x2 + ...

and you want their difference for two different values, which I
understand as

	exp(beta_x1 * x1.new <http://x1.new> ) - exp(beta_x2 * x2.new <http://x2.new>)

?

In this case, you can just use

	fun = function(x1.new <http://x1.new>, x2.new <http://x2.new>) {
		return (exp(x1 * x1.new <http://x1.new>) - exp(x2 * x2.new <http://x2.new>))
	}

and then pass 'x1.new <http://x1.new>' and x2.new <http://x2.new> as arguments to
inla.posterior.function.eval()

let me know

H

Hi everyone. I have one question regarding a negative binomial regression with a random error in the linear predictor. This is the setup:

library(INLA)

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Weird results with nbinomial regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm not quite sure what exactly is 'weird', I am not surprised about
the results.

The negative binomial can be reinterpreted as poisson regression with
an added (independent) random effect

	y ~ 1 + ... + u

where u_i is loggamma distributed, and if you integrated u_i out,
you'll get the nbinomial.

adding another (indep) random effect, like

	y ~ 1 + ... + u + v

then, with single observation, you only observe one observation for
each u_i+v_i, so only the prior (essentially) determine what is 'u' and
what is 'v', since only their sum is likelihood identifiable.

with replication, your size 3, then j=1..3, so you observe

	u_i1 + v_i
	u_i2 + v_i
	u_i3 + v_i

which means that identfication of what is 'u' and what is 'v' is now
much much easier.

H

Tomas

messages.subject: SPDE and Prediction in Zero-Inflated Poisson
messages.subject_clean: SPDE and Prediction in Zero-Inflated Poisson
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
There are some very helpful threads floating around here on zero-inflation prediction, but I have a few item I could not resolve by reviewing those. I’ve attempted to construct a zero-inflated Poisson model. I’ve created a fully reproducible example using a dummy dataset. The R file should be "click and run"

Here are some questions I’m looking for advice on:
1. The data is originally in decimal degree lat/lon. The area of interest spans several UTM regions, which precludes that as a projection option. I understand UTM to be one of the better projections for measuring distance, and I read in the SPDE gitbook that lat/lon is in appropriate for spatial models (with gaussian random fields). Additionally, following your “Bayesian Spatial Modelling with R-INLA” example paper, I decided to work directly on the spherical mesh. My question is this: Is this the most accurate way to calculate the gaussian spatial random field, and is the general process I pursue to accomplish this correct?

2. In my code, there are 882 mesh nodes, 1,000 training datapoints, 1,000 test datapoints (See: length(INLA_model$summary.fitted.values$mean)   ). Yet there are 4,000 fitted values, and seems to vary (the original data has around 4,442 fitted values despite essentially being the same setup). Notably, the predictions for some of these mystery points are quite massive. Perhaps they are for mesh nodes with no covariates, confusing the model. The challenge here is that it makes it difficult to specify the “link” argument since I don’t know before-hand how long the prediction vector is. How  do I understand where these extra fitted values are coming from?

3. Most importantly,  I seem to be struggling to get the fitted values for the model, or at least ones that make sense. I’ve included tables/plots demonstrating the issue in the final two code chunks. Please note that I’m using the “Naïve” approach for now to get approximate results (I hope). I will follow examples on this forum to get more theoretically valid predictions.
a. In other questions I’ve read on this forum, people add link=1 for the testing set because the default is the identity link when the response is missing. But my responses appear to be in terms of counts and do not change to when I add link=c(rep(1,1000),rep(NA,1000)) . How is this possible?
b. It would seem that 1’s are “inflated”. Perhaps it is bad model fit, but my guess is that I have made an error. Any idea why this might be?

Note: The following are items I am planning to address, so no need to address these as of now, unless of course you think they are related to my issues above:
- Lack of prior specification, especially for matern function
- Mesh needs refinement (extent is needlessly large)

INLA is an amazing package—I had been unsuccessfully attempting to fit spatial models for this large dataset (this is only a sample) for several months using other packages. It’s wonderfully fast and stable! If there is anything I can to do make these questions easier to answer, I’m happy to oblige.

Regards,
Mark

library(tidyverse)
library(INLA)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(inlabru)
library(gridExtra)
library(sf)

#Read in data
INLA_train_masked<-read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/millermc38/Research/master/INLA_train_masked.csv")%>%select(-X1)%>%mutate(x15=round(x15))
INLA_test_masked<-read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/millermc38/Research/master/INLA_test_masked.csv")%>%
  select(-X1)%>%mutate(x15=round(x15))
#You should be able to ignore the warnings safely

#Get wisconsin sf object, extract coordinates, and project them directly on the globe
wisconsin_sf<-st_as_sf(ne_download(scale = 50, type = "states"))%>%
  filter(code_hasc=="US.WI")
coords<-st_coordinates(wisconsin_sf)
coords_cartesion = inla.mesh.map(coords, projection = "longlat")

# Construct mesh for the state
boundary.loc <- SpatialPoints(as.matrix(coords_cartesion))
boundary <- list(
  inla.nonconvex.hull(coordinates(boundary.loc), 0.012),
  inla.nonconvex.hull(coordinates(boundary.loc), 0.0265))
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=boundary,
                     max.edge=c(0.0044, 0.0266),
                     min.angle=c(20, 18),
                     max.n=c(48000, 16000), ## Safeguard against large meshes.
                     max.n.strict=c(128000, 128000), ## Don't build a huge mesh!
                     cutoff=0.001, ## Filter away adjacent points.
                     offset=c(0.012, 0.0265)) ## Offset for extra boundaries, if needed.

#Review the plot. It's larger than it needs to be--I'll fix that  later.
ggplot()+
  gg(mesh)+#This uses inlabru package
  geom_point(aes(x=coords_cartesion[,1],y=coords_cartesion[,2]))+
  labs(title="Constrained refined Delaunay triangulation",
       x="3D Cartesian X",y="3D Cartesian Y")+
  theme_bw()

#Let's make a mesh and an index
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh, alpha=2)
s_index = inla.spde.make.index(name = "spatial.field",
                               spde$n.spde)

#Identify lat/lon in the training set, convert them to cartesian, make A Matrix, make train stack
coords_train <- as.matrix(INLA_train_masked%>%select(x16,x17))
coords_cartesian_train = inla.mesh.map(coords_train, projection = "longlat")
A_matrix_train = inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh, loc=coords_cartesian_train)
train_stack <- inla.stack(data = list(x15 = INLA_train_masked$x15),
                          A = list(A_matrix_train, 1),
                          effects = list(c(s_index, list(intercept = 1)),
                                         list(cov = INLA_train_masked%>%select(-c(x15:x17)))), #Remove lat, lon, response
                          tag = "train")

#Same as above, but now for the test set
coords_test <- as.matrix(INLA_test_masked%>%select(x16,x17))
coords_cartesion_test = inla.mesh.map(coords_test, projection = "longlat")
A_matrix_test = inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh, loc=coords_cartesion_test)
test_stack <- inla.stack(data = list(x15 = NA),
                         A = list(A_matrix_test, 1),
                         effects = list(c(s_index, list(intercept = 1)),
                                        list(cov = INLA_test_masked%>%select(-c(x15:x17)))), #Remove lat, lon, response
                         tag = "test")

#Combine train/test stacks
INLA_stacks <- inla.stack(train_stack, test_stack)

#Model Formula. Basically: x15 ~ x1+...+X14+spatial.field (x16 is lat, x17 is lon, so leave those off)
inla_formula<-str_c("-1","intercept",paste0(names(INLA_train_masked)[-c(15:17)],collapse = "+"),"f(spatial.field, model=spde)",sep = "+")%>%str_c("x15~",.)%>%as.formula()

#Model. I have four logical processors, and that usually takes around 45 seconds to run this block
INLA_model <- inla(inla_formula,
                   family = "zeroinflatedpoisson1",
                   data = inla.stack.data(INLA_stacks, spde=spde),
                   control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(INLA_stacks),
                                          compute=TRUE),
                   control.compute=list(config = TRUE)) #to try inlabru predict function
#link=c(rep(1,1000),rep(NA,1000)) does not seem to change the outcome

#Store theta
zero_prob<-summary(INLA_model)[["hyperpar"]][1,1]
one_m_zero_prob<-(1-zero_prob)

#Extract "naive" fitted values for training set, create various summaries
train_index = inla.stack.index(INLA_stacks, "train")$data
train_fit<-(INLA_model$summary.fitted.values$mean[train_index])*one_m_zero_prob
cor(INLA_train_masked$x15,
    train_fit)
train_fit%>%summary
table(round(train_fit))
grid.arrange(ggplot()+geom_histogram(aes(x=train_fit),binwidth = 1),
             ggplot()+geom_histogram(data=INLA_train_masked,aes(x=x15),binwidth = 1))

#Extract "naive" fitted values for testing set, create various summaries
test_index = inla.stack.index(INLA_stacks, "test")$data
test_fit<-(INLA_model$summary.fitted.values$mean[test_index])*one_m_zero_prob
cor(INLA_test_masked$x15,
    test_fit)
test_fit%>%summary
table(round(test_fit))
grid.arrange(ggplot()+geom_histogram(aes(x=test_fit),binwidth = 1),
             ggplot()+geom_histogram(data=INLA_test_masked,aes(x=x15),binwidth = 1))

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,
I can only answers some of this at this time:

1) If a stationary field on (part of) the globe is a reasonable model,
then yes, building it directly on the sphere is a good idea.
  You can/should take advantage of the fact that the mesh routines
know about CRS information, so instead of transforming coordinates
yourself, you can
  supply the coordinates in whatever format you have them (although
with several UTM inputs, transforming to a common coordinate system
first is practical, which seems like you've don, to longlat?).
You then also need to tell inla.mesh.2d what CRS to build the mesh in,
and there is a shortcut defined for that, crs=inla.CRS("sphere").
That will make it build a sphere with unit radius, so all distances
will be in radians. You have to take that into account when specifying
max.edge values; divide actual metres by the earth radius (around
3.6e6 I believe) to get the corresponding radian distance.
Just as you do now, you can supply nonconvex boundary information;
just make sure to set a crs when you build those, so it can transform
them onto the sphere.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
See below:

On Mon, 20 Apr 2020 at 13:20, Tomas T. <tomas.t...@gmail.com> wrote:
> 1) You recommended against something and referred to Lindgren & Rue
> ... which is not referring to the pcmatern prior. I just want to make
> sure I understand this correctly - so is it recommended to use the
> prior described in Fuglstad 2019 (see screenshot) - i.e. the
> inla.spde2.pcmatern? I guess the answer is yes, I just want to clear
> possible confusions :)

Worst: inla.spde2.matern with default parameters
Better: inla.spde2.matern with more sensible parameters, as in Lindgren&Rue.
Best: inla.spde2.pcmatern with sensibly chosen parameters, as in Fuglstad 2019

> 2) In my current application (my own code, not using INLA), I am using
> Matern with v = 3/2, which has nice simplification and is easy to
> compute. When I look into INLA, maximum alpha I can use is 2, and d=2,
> which means that maximum v possible (and the default value) in INLA is
> v = alpha - d/2 = 1? Is that correct?

In d=2, nu=3/2 isn't a Markov field, so needs other approximations,
which we've only directly implemented
up to alpha=2 (0 < nu <=1).
You can use the equations in the Authors' response to the 2011
Lindgren et al SPDE/GRMF to
implement the fractional models for higher alpha values as an rgeneric model.
But the higher nu values quickly become hard to distinguish from each other.
Whether the difference between nu = 1 and nu = 3/2 is important
depends on your problem.
Much spatial statistics uses nu = 1/2 (which is Markov in 1D and 3D
but not in 2D), but I'd
argue that that's largely due to convenience, just as your 3/2 case.

> So you most of the times use v = 1? Up to now I've seen papers to use
> Matern with v = 3/2; do you have any comparison with that?

I don't, others may have.

> 3) The definition of the joint PC prior (see the screenshot) doesn't
> seem to depend on the parameter v, am I right? So do you think it
> could be used even with the value of v = 3/2, if I want to keep my old
> function?

I don't recall the specifics, but it may be applicable, yes. I do
think there's a dimension dependence,
and the range and variance are linked to nu, so there may be hidden
dependencies.
Would need to check the details of the Fuglstad paper.

Finn

>
> Tomas

> > For pc-prior for SPDE matern models, see
> > ?inla.spde.pcmatern
> > By design, that one doesn’t have any default parameters for the prior.
> > The documentation explains the parameters.
> >
> > The inla.spde.matern models use a log-gaussian prior for tau and kappa, with prior mean zero. I recommend agains using the default parameters (that feature is only still there for backwards compatibility). Instead, see the approach in the journal of statistical software, Lindgren&Rue “Bayesian Spatial Modelling with R-INLA”.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all working with INLA

First of all thanks for your time

I am wondering if DIC  values (or any others, waic) could be used as an indicator of good performance to compare among models with different families of distribution (Poisson vs Gaussian)?

or maybe DIC or waic values should be used to compare models with the same family of distribution, for instance, just models constructed with a Poisson distribution ?

The questions are because I am looking at which factors or factor explain mainly my response variable more than to do any prediction. My response variable is number or organisms in the field (count data) . I think that I could do at least two alternatives

(a) run models with a Poisson distribution, maybe with an “offset” of Volume of water: M5= Poisson (GLM) and M6=Poisson (GLM + spatial random)

(b) or models with a Gaussian distribution with density (count/volume of water): M1 = Gaussian (explanatory variables with rw1), M2= Gaussian (explanatory variables with  rw2), M3 = Gaussian (explanatory variables with rw1) + spde, and  M4 = Gaussian (explanatory variables with rw2) + spde

So, could I compare models with same fixed variables but running with different family via DIC values? For instance, M5, M1 and M2  or  between M3, M4, and M6.

Or just I should compare M5 with M6? And models within the group M1-M4?

The other question is about how I could include the offset variable in a Poisson model. should be introduced in the model in this way?

M5 M6  <- inla(formula, offset=CTD$LogVol , family = "poisson",  data = inla.stack.data(stk2),  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk2)))

Thanks so much

Quique

Dear Quique,

Yes, you can use DIC or WAIC (more recommended) to compare models. You can use them to compare models using the same data and response variable. You can use them to compare different distributions, but then compare models with the same model structure (covariates). And compare sensible distributions e.g. Poisson with zero-inflated Poisson or negative binomial. Comparing Poisson with Gaussian doesn't make sense IMHO.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Quique,

IMHO, the distribution should match the data generating process. Counts originate from a discrete distribution, making the Gaussian distribution unsuitable, especially with low counts.

You have three options for defining an offset: the 'offset' argument, the 'E' argument or adding it as a covariate and give its parameter a highly informative prior to fix it close to 1. Note that you want to use log(Volume) as an offset when the distribution uses a log link.

Best regards,

ir. Thierry Onkelinx

messages.body_plain:
Finn,

Please hold off on answering my other questions. I realized that my predicted/fitted values, at least for the training set, are correct (if I am reading the documentation right) and don't need to be multiplied by 1-theta ( I was following another thread I thought was the same question as mine, but was not). Really all that remains for me to figure out is why the model fits so many one's, so I'm trying a hurdle model to see if it is a model specification problem.

Regards,

Mark

On Monday, April 20, 2020 at 10:36:18 AM UTC-4, Mark wrote:
> Hello,
> There are some very helpful threads floating around here on zero-inflation prediction, but I have a few item I could not resolve by reviewing those. I’ve attempted to construct a zero-inflated Poisson model. I’ve created a fully reproducible example using a dummy dataset. The R file should be "click and run"
>
> Here are some questions I’m looking for advice on:
> 1. The data is originally in decimal degree lat/lon. The area of interest spans several UTM regions, which precludes that as a projection option. I understand UTM to be one of the better projections for measuring distance, and I read in the SPDE gitbook that lat/lon is in appropriate for spatial models (with gaussian random fields). Additionally, following your “Bayesian Spatial Modelling with R-INLA” example paper, I decided to work directly on the spherical mesh. My question is this: Is this the most accurate way to calculate the gaussian spatial random field, and is the general process I pursue to accomplish this correct?
>
> 2. In my code, there are 882 mesh nodes, 1,000 training datapoints, 1,000 test datapoints (See: length(INLA_model$summary.fitted.values$mean)   ). Yet there are 4,000 fitted values, and seems to vary (the original data has around 4,442 fitted values despite essentially being the same setup). Notably, the predictions for some of these mystery points are quite massive. Perhaps they are for mesh nodes with no covariates, confusing the model. The challenge here is that it makes it difficult to specify the “link” argument since I don’t know before-hand how long the prediction vector is. How  do I understand where these extra fitted values are coming from?
>
> 3. Most importantly,  I seem to be struggling to get the fitted values for the model, or at least ones that make sense. I’ve included tables/plots demonstrating the issue in the final two code chunks. Please note that I’m using the “Naïve” approach for now to get approximate results (I hope). I will follow examples on this forum to get more theoretically valid predictions.
> a. In other questions I’ve read on this forum, people add link=1 for the testing set because the default is the identity link when the response is missing. But my responses appear to be in terms of counts and do not change to when I add link=c(rep(1,1000),rep(NA,1000)) . How is this possible?
> b. It would seem that 1’s are “inflated”. Perhaps it is bad model fit, but my guess is that I have made an error. Any idea why this might be?
>
> Note: The following are items I am planning to address, so no need to address these as of now, unless of course you think they are related to my issues above:
> - Lack of prior specification, especially for matern function
> - Mesh needs refinement (extent is needlessly large)
>
> INLA is an amazing package—I had been unsuccessfully attempting to fit spatial models for this large dataset (this is only a sample) for several months using other packages. It’s wonderfully fast and stable! If there is anything I can to do make these questions easier to answer, I’m happy to oblige.
>
> Regards,
> Mark
>
> library(tidyverse)
> library(INLA)
> library(rnaturalearth)
> library(inlabru)
> library(gridExtra)
> library(sf)
>
> #Read in data
> INLA_train_masked<-read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/millermc38/Research/master/INLA_train_masked.csv")%>%select(-X1)%>%mutate(x15=round(x15))
> INLA_test_masked<-read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/millermc38/Research/master/INLA_test_masked.csv")%>%
>   select(-X1)%>%mutate(x15=round(x15))
> #You should be able to ignore the warnings safely
>
> #Get wisconsin sf object, extract coordinates, and project them directly on the globe
> wisconsin_sf<-st_as_sf(ne_download(scale = 50, type = "states"))%>%
>   filter(code_hasc=="US.WI")
> coords<-st_coordinates(wisconsin_sf)
> coords_cartesion = inla.mesh.map(coords, projection = "longlat")
>
> # Construct mesh for the state
> boundary.loc <- SpatialPoints(as.matrix(coords_cartesion))
> boundary <- list(
>   inla.nonconvex.hull(coordinates(boundary.loc), 0.012),
>   inla.nonconvex.hull(coordinates(boundary.loc), 0.0265))
> mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=boundary,
>                      max.edge=c(0.0044, 0.0266),
>                      min.angle=c(20, 18),
>                      max.n=c(48000, 16000), ## Safeguard against large meshes.
>                      max.n.strict=c(128000, 128000), ## Don't build a huge mesh!
>                      cutoff=0.001, ## Filter away adjacent points.
>                      offset=c(0.012, 0.0265)) ## Offset for extra boundaries, if needed.
>
> #Review the plot. It's larger than it needs to be--I'll fix that  later.
> ggplot()+
>   gg(mesh)+#This uses inlabru package
>   geom_point(aes(x=coords_cartesion[,1],y=coords_cartesion[,2]))+
>   labs(title="Constrained refined Delaunay triangulation",
>        x="3D Cartesian X",y="3D Cartesian Y")+
>   theme_bw()
>
> #Let's make a mesh and an index
> spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh, alpha=2)
> s_index = inla.spde.make.index(name = "spatial.field",
>                                spde$n.spde)
>
> #Identify lat/lon in the training set, convert them to cartesian, make A Matrix, make train stack
> coords_train <- as.matrix(INLA_train_masked%>%select(x16,x17))
> coords_cartesian_train = inla.mesh.map(coords_train, projection = "longlat")
> A_matrix_train = inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh, loc=coords_cartesian_train)
> train_stack <- inla.stack(data = list(x15 = INLA_train_masked$x15),
>                           A = list(A_matrix_train, 1),
>                           effects = list(c(s_index, list(intercept = 1)),
>                                          list(cov = INLA_train_masked%>%select(-c(x15:x17)))), #Remove lat, lon, response
>                           tag = "train")
>
> #Same as above, but now for the test set
> coords_test <- as.matrix(INLA_test_masked%>%select(x16,x17))
> coords_cartesion_test = inla.mesh.map(coords_test, projection = "longlat")
> A_matrix_test = inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh, loc=coords_cartesion_test)
> test_stack <- inla.stack(data = list(x15 = NA),
>                          A = list(A_matrix_test, 1),
>                          effects = list(c(s_index, list(intercept = 1)),
>                                         list(cov = INLA_test_masked%>%select(-c(x15:x17)))), #Remove lat, lon, response
>                          tag = "test")
>
> #Combine train/test stacks
> INLA_stacks <- inla.stack(train_stack, test_stack)
>
> #Model Formula. Basically: x15 ~ x1+...+X14+spatial.field (x16 is lat, x17 is lon, so leave those off)
> inla_formula<-str_c("-1","intercept",paste0(names(INLA_train_masked)[-c(15:17)],collapse = "+"),"f(spatial.field, model=spde)",sep = "+")%>%str_c("x15~",.)%>%as.formula()
>
> #Model. I have four logical processors, and that usually takes around 45 seconds to run this block
> INLA_model <- inla(inla_formula,
>                    family = "zeroinflatedpoisson1",
>                    data = inla.stack.data(INLA_stacks, spde=spde),
>                    control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(INLA_stacks),
>                                           compute=TRUE),
>                    control.compute=list(config = TRUE)) #to try inlabru predict function
> #link=c(rep(1,1000),rep(NA,1000)) does not seem to change the outcome
>
> #Store theta
> zero_prob<-summary(INLA_model)[["hyperpar"]][1,1]
> one_m_zero_prob<-(1-zero_prob)
>
> #Extract "naive" fitted values for training set, create various summaries
> train_index = inla.stack.index(INLA_stacks, "train")$data

messages.subject: question about iid model
messages.subject_clean: question about iid model
messages.body_plain:
May I ask a possibly dumb question? I thought I'd
understood the basics of INLA model specification,
but now I'm not sure.

Let y be an n-vector of observations, and x an n-vector of
covariates in data frame 'd1'.

Now consider the model

m1<-inla(y~x,data=d1)

As I understand it, this is equivalent to the
formal specification

y = b0 + b1*x + u
u~N(0,tI)

where I is the n*n identity matrix, and we have
default priors on b0, b1 and t. In other words,
u is an iid error term, which we can consider
to be an iid random effect. Is this right?

Now define d1$ID<-1:nrow(d1) so that ID is 1:n,
and consider the model

m2<-inla(y~x+f(ID,model="iid"), data=d1)

My question is: aren't we adding a second random effect
that's exactly like the first one? What's the formal
specification corresponding to m2?  I could see the point
if, eg, we had a longitudinal dataset, so that elements of
ID would be repeated; but that's not the case in my example.
>From the documentation: "This model simply defines [the r.e]
to be a vector of independent and Gaussian distributed random
variable (possibly scaled) with precision [tau]". Isn't there
an identification issue here, if we combine it with the
default Gaussian?

In fact, if I define (following slm.pdf)

zero.variance = list(prec=list(initial = 11, fixed=TRUE))

and then run

m3<-inla(y~x+f(ID,model="iid"), data=d1,
    control.family = list(hyper=zero.variance))

it looks as though m3 is the same as m1, which seems to confirm that
f(ID, model="iid") duplicates the Gaussian error in m1. Any clarification
very gratefully received.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] question about iid model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] question about iid model
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your email. You're right, the normal response model, like

y = a + b * x + epsilon

and be considered as a model with random effect, but then with exact
observations. what is random effect and what is not, is not well
defined.

if you want to fit the model

	a + b * x + u

for iid random effect u, where the i'th observation is

	a + b * x[i] + u[i]

with exact observations, then you have to fix the precision in the
likelihood to a high value.

If both are unknown, like precision of u, and the precision in the
likelihood, then you'll have like

	u[i] + epsilon[i]

so you observe just the sum in the likelihood, and you have to
determine (using priors) what goes to u and what goes to epsilon.

However, often you'll have replication so that

formula = y ~ 1 + x + f(idx, model="iid)

but we have repeated measurements for the same random effect, like

	idx = rep(1:3, each = n %/% 3)

if each where observered 3 times. this gives you enough information to
separate 'u' from 'epsilon', and estimate both the precision parameter
in the likelihood and u

like

n = 99
m = 3
idx = rep(1:m, each = n/m)
u = rnorm(m)
x = rnorm(n)
y = 1 + x + u[idx] + rnorm(n, sd=0.1)
r = inla(y ~ 1 + x + f(idx),
         data = data.frame(y, x, idx))
summary(r)

H

messages.subject: Shouldn't log likelihood always be normalized by data size in bayesian estimation?
messages.subject_clean: Shouldn't log likelihood always be normalized by data size in bayesian estimation?
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

This is a general question which applies to bayesian statistics in
general, and I wonder how INLA deals with this.

INLA also has penalized complexity priors. But, the magnitude of the
PC prior will not change with data size; while the magnitude of log
likelihood will!

Please follow the details of the questions in here:
https://stats.stackexchange.com/q/462076/5509

This is something I am wrapping my head around for some time and I
need some help on this. I would be grateful for answer on general
statistical level, as well as how INLA deals with this.

Thanks and have a great day!

Tomas

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Shouldn't log likelihood always be normalized by data size in bayesian estimation?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Shouldn't log likelihood always be normalized by data size in bayesian estimation?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tomas,

no, the premise of the stackexchange question is incorrect.

Yes, the size of the log-likelihood depends on the number of
observations, but that's precisely what should happen; the more data
you have, the less influence the prior should have; otherwise
collecting more date would be useless, and we'd never gain more
knowledge than if we collected only one observation.
(Also, the actual magnitude of the likelihood isn't really what's
important for this, it's how the values depend on the parameters, but
in this case that works out in the same way.)

This is no different from frequentist likelihood estimation, where the
uncertainty estimates (in asymptotic cases) comes from the hessian of
the loglikelihood, that also scales linearly in the number of
observation, showing that the uncertainty decreases the more
observations we use (since the uncertainty is represented by the the
inverse of the hessian, the estimator covariance approximation, and
that variance scales as 1/n)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA group,

I have been trying to generalize the case of the orthogonal spatial restrains in discrete time spatio-temporal model for point data, and I'm running on implementation difficulties specifically linked with the indexing. I have run through Daniels spatial restrains script as well as the tutorial spatio-temporal cases separatelly, but I was wondering if the two can be merged.

Bellow is are the essential parts of the script at it's current state:

  # xmat # dataset with covariates and outcome, we have k distinct time periods.

  # Projeciton matrix
  A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = as.matrix(xmat[, c("x", "y")]), group = xmat$time, n.group = k)
  spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2, prior.range = prior.range, prior.sigma = prior.sigma, constr = T)
  w_field <- inla.spde.make.index(name = "w", n.spde = spde$n.spde, n.group = k)

  n.data <- nrow(xmat)
  #fixed_effects # vector with names of fixed effects
  n.covariates <- length(fixed_effects)

  # QR for the design matrix'
  Q <- qr.Q(qr(xmat[, fixed_effects])) #includes Intercept

  # Linear constrained effects
  A.constr <- list(A = as.matrix(t(Q)%*%A), e = rep(0,n.covariates))

  # temporal AR(1) dependence
  h.spec <- list(model = 'ar1', hyper = list(theta = list(prior = 'pccor1', param = c(0, 0.9))))

  #Stack
  stk <- inla.stack(data = list(Y = xmat$positives, N = xmat$sample_size),
                        A = list(A, 1),
                        tag = 'fitted',
                        effects = list(w_field, data.frame(xmat[, c(fixed_effects, "epsilon")])))# epsilon = 1:nrow(xmat) # noise

   fit.idx  <- inla.stack.index(stk.fit, tag = "fitted")$data

f1 <- as.formula(c("Y ~ 0 + Intercept + V1 + V2 + V3 + V4 + V5 +
  f(w, model = spde, extraconstr = A.constr, group = w.group, control.group = h.spec) +
  f(epsilon, model = 'iid')"))

result <- inla(formula = f1, data = inla.stack.data(stk),
                 family = "binomial",
                 Ntrials = inla.stack.data(stk)$N,
                 control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1, A = inla.stack.A(stk)),
                 control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, dic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE, config = TRUE),
                 control.inla = list(correct = TRUE, int.strategy = "eb", strategy = "gaussian"),

When I run the above I get the following error:
Error in inla(formula = formula, data = inla.stack.data(stk), family = family,  :

    ncol in matrix A(extraconstr) does not correspont to the length of f: 64332 32166
###.###

I haven't had any troubles for the spatio-temporal case without confounding. Likewise the case of confounding with a single spatial process works well for simulated data and I retrieve the models parameters. I believe there is an issue on my code on the grouping variables between spde and A...

I have also hard coded the orthogonal constrains within inside the spde model but still the same issue persists.

Thank you for reading this and for any possible suggestions.

I would like to apply the orthogonal spatial confounding for each group (timepoint) instead of an average over all timepoints.

messages.subject: Identification of Spatial Confounding
messages.subject_clean: Identification of Spatial Confounding
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA group,

I have a question related to identify spatial confounding. In my case study, I am addressing the effect of livestock grazing pressure on the space use by a steppe-bird species. The response variable and the covariate are measured at large spatial scales, and they are expected to be spatially correlated. If I fit a non-spatial gaussian model, grazing pressure has an important effect on the use of space by the steppe-bird species. However, this effect disappears when I fit a spatial model to my data.

In order to justify the implementation of a linear orthogonality constraint (i.e., a restricted spatial regression model) I have proceeded as follows:

First, I have fitted the spatial model incorporating the covariates of interest as predictors. In this model, as I explained above, the covariates did not have an effect on my response variable (i.e., space use).
Secondly, I have obtained the u_i values for each observation and I have fitted a non-spatial model incorporating the covariates of interests as predictors. If the covariates had an important effect on u_i, then I have considered that there are evidences of spatial confounding, supporting the constraint of the spatial random effect to be orthogonal to the fixed effects.
Lastly, I have fitted the spatial model imposing a linear orthogonality constraint using the argument extraconstr= in INLA

Is this procedure reasonable? Does it justify the implementation of the spatial constrains? Are there other procedures to identify spatial confounding? I am aware that the multicollinearity among spatial covariates and the spatial random effect may hide the effect of fixed predictors important under a non-spatial linear model. Nevertheless, I am equally concerned about the implementation of constrains because this model may yield 95%BCI for the regression parameter without overlapping zero, when that regression parameter is truly zero (i.e., Type-S error).

On the other hand, can I compare two spatial models (with and without constraints) using wAIC? If the spatial model without constraints has a lower wAIC values, does it mean that I shouldn’t impose orthogonality constraints? My reasoning is that I cannot compare both models because I am imposing constraints to one of those to be able to detect important effects, but I am not fully sure about this.

Thank you very much for your time and apologize if your consider that this is not the proper place for this topic.

Best,

Julia

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

> Havard: Thanks for your quick and helpful reply. The reason I asked
> the question was that I was reading ch 7.2.2 (Spatial Models)
> of the online book "Bayesian Inference with INLA"
> (https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-spatial.html#sec:irrlattice)
> and it appeared to me that in model boston.iid (a preparatory
> non-spatial model) the author had done just that:
> added an iid random effect to a standard iid-Gaussian
> regression model; and I didn't see what was gained.

As Håvard said, my aim here was to show how to fit different models. The problem (that I realized now!) is that with a Gaussian likelihood you do not want any extra iid effect in the linear predictor.  Note also that the ‘bym’ model includes an iid term as well. I have usually fit these models for disease mapping using a Poisson likelihood, which is probably why I did not think twice about some of them. In the case of a Poisson likelihood, all models make sense and having an ‘iid’ term will help to model overdispersion.

However, you could still use ‘iid’ random effect with a Gaussian likelihood if you have groups in the data (such as in the multilevel models explained in the book) because the random effect is estimated using different observations.

So, the examples show how to fit different models but I agree with Håvard that some of ’these aren't the models you're looking for’.

Thanks for the feedback. I’ll make sure that this is fixed in the book.

Best,

Virgilio

messages.subject: Spatial replicates, versus repeated measures random effect on the same site?
messages.subject_clean: Spatial replicates, versus repeated measures random effect on the same site?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Discussion group,

Could someone elucidate the difference between using "formula = y ~ -1 + intercept + f(spatial, model=spde, replicate=spatial.repl)", for 2 measurements at the same location, and using "formula = y ~ -1 + intercept + f(ID, model='iid') + f(spatial, model=spde)" ?

Using the second formula, one can obtain both residual variance ( transformed precision of gaussian observations) and precision for the repeated measurements, alongside the spatial variance and range. Using the first formula, the precision on repeated measures seem to be incorporated in the spatial variance?

Is one specification preferred above the other? Given I would like to use Variance_ID/(Variance_Residual + Variance_Spatial + Variance_ID) as a measure for repeatability?

best wishes and thanks in advance for any comments,
Vincent

Finn

I attach a simple simulated example to show my case (please pardon my rather unsofisticated script).

My biggest concern is with regards to the uncertainty. "Fitted value" results are much sharper than those obtained by using inla.posterior.sample or inla.rmarginal. Also inla.rmarginal seems to consistently give larger estimates than inla.posterior.sample.

Any thoughts? I may be doing something very silly in which case I strongly apologize...

Best,
iosu

A couple of things:

You seem to have a typo on this line:
covar_idx = which(sample$covar[example_idx] == fit$summary.random$covar[,1])
The variable you created at the top is called samples, not sample; check what you actually get as covar_idx from this line.

The distribution of a sum of independent rmarginal values should not be the same as the sum of effects simulated by posterior.sample, since the latter takes the posterior dependence into account (which can be considerable).

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

just to follow up. By construction, the inla.posterior.sample() will
not give presicely the same marginals that inla() computes. Its getting
a bit technical, but with the most recent testing version, we're
*almost* there, while `we' have managed to keep the extra computational
cost negligible. (We = a PhD student here, Cristian Chiuchiolo).

The inla.posterior.sample() have now the argument 'skew.corr' that is
default TRUE, that will correct for skewness assuming a SkewNormal
marginal for each component in the mixture, and do the mapping from the
Normal to SkewNormal using a two-dimensional pre-computed table of
mapping functions. This is what keeps the cost low.

Of course its possible to maintain the marginals as well, at the cost
of higher computational costs, but I think finding a good balance is
the key.

H

messages.subject: RE: [r-inla] Can the variables in INLA-SPDE can be categorical?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can the variables in INLA-SPDE can be categorical?
messages.body_plain:
As I understand these questions:

Yes
Yes, in the sense that you can have non-spatial covariates generally; technically the spde covariates tend to take continuous inputs but sometimes they can be binned along their continuums for smoothing purposes;
I have not had this be a problem.  If multicollinearity is a concern with fixed effects, you can certainly adjust the priors and/or use ridge regression to force the predictive parameter space to make sharper decisions about how the coefficients are allocated. For latent effects (random effects, etc.) collinearity is rarely a serious concern.  If necessary to tease out additional effects, you can use nesting or varying slopes. Nesting is less computationally expensive and often works just as well if not better.

Jonathan

Mark

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] What's the default prior for fixed effect?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] What's the default prior for fixed effect?
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 2020-04-28 at 17:42 -0700, Mark wrote:
> When the intercept is explicitly included in the covariates (e.g.
> y~0+intercept+x1+....xn), for example in the Advanced example
> starting on page 9 of the INLA documentation (
> https://inla.r-inla-download.org/r-inla.org/doc/likelihood/zeroinflated.pdf
> ), should the intercept be manually set to N(0,0), or is it okay at
> N(0,.001)?  The intercepts are N(0,.001) in that example.

the default prior for the intercept (ie the +1 in the formula, which is
also default added), is N(0,precision=0). you can change that using

control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = A)

to set the precision to be A.

you can set the precision for other fixed effects in control.fixed as
well, see ?control.fixed.

there is an easier interface with f(w,model="linear"), see
inla.doc("linear"), that makes it easier to define prior mean,prec, for
a spesific fixed effect. Note that this f()-model is just a wrapper, so
other features like 'replicate', etc are not defined for this one.

> Also, as I type this, I'm realizing that for SPDE, we manually take
> out the intercept with "-1" and in the example above, we take it out
> with "0". After playing around with the example code, they seem
> equivalent, so I'm curious as to why we sometimes use "-1" and
> sometimes "0"

that part is parsed similar to lm() using their code, and

	-1 + ...

is eqv to

	0 + ...

H

--

messages.body_plain:
All Gaussian model components can be represented in rgeneric.

in your case, you'll have two 'graphs', one that is for the precision
matrix, and one for L.

the rgeneric defines Q (precision matrix), so you have to compute that
one from their representation. its like LL', depending on how you
define L.

just make sure you define L to be a sparse matrix, so that L %*% t(L)
is sparse as well.

you can use Q to define the graph, unless some of its elements is zero
that is later non-zero.

H
